headline.lead: Three years out, a blend of no change, faded growth and the sector's growth misses actual revenue by a median 17%, and a range built from past misses held the outcome 82% of the time at 80% and 93% at 90%.
headline.sub: Against assuming no change, the blend had 7% less error (t = 5.1); fading the company's own growth, a common DCF starting point, had 1% more error (t = 0.6, not a real difference); extrapolating that growth straight had 23% more error (t = 6.6). A range from a ±3-point wobble in growth held only 14% against the 80% it implies.

findings.label: H1 supported
findings.text: For the fastest growers (top tenth, median prior growth 27%), the faded-growth forecast ran 23% too high three years out (t = 3.7); for the slowest tenth, 27% too low. The blend ran 4% too low for the fastest growers (t = -0.8).

findings.label: H2 supported
findings.text: Three years out, holding last year's operating margin missed by a median 2.8 points against 2.9 for the three-year average (t = -1.3, negative favors the average).

findings.label: H3 partly supported
findings.text: The simulated P10–P90 range held the outcome 14% of the time one year out and 14% five years out, against the 80% it implies. Misses fell 45% below the range and 41% above it three years out.

practice.title: Draw ranges from past misses, not from a growth wobble.
practice.text: A ±3-point band in growth held 14% of outcomes three years out. Quantiles of past forecast errors, scaled to the company's volatility, held 82% at 80%, reaching a median 28% below and 42% above the forecast. Honest ranges are wide.

practice.title: Don't trust recent high growth.
practice.text: For companies growing a median 27% a year, a faded-growth forecast ran 23% too high three years out. Pull the starting rate toward no change and the sector.

practice.title: Start from the blend.
practice.text: The geometric mean of no change, the faded trend and the sector beat the fade alone at every horizon from 1 to 5 years, and beat no change by 7% three years out (t = 5.1). Depart from it only with company-specific evidence.

practice.title: Beat no change first.
practice.text: Three years out, fading the company's own growth was not measurably better than assuming revenue stays flat: 1% more error (t = 0.6, not a real difference). Argue any growth story against that baseline.

valuation_model: Revenue ranges in the DCF simulation are drawn from this study's calibrated error table.
The default DCF's base case for years 1–5 is the blend.
Every DCF shows the value with revenue held flat beside it.
